_note: Every fact in light.json 'facts' and every dataset in data/ points at keys here. 'checked' says what was read and when. Raw copies of each page and file are in .refs/light/ (tools/light_fetch.py, git-ignored). 'licence' is given for every dataset the page ships.

codata-h.cite: NIST, CODATA Value: Planck constant (2022 CODATA recommended values).
codata-h.checked: 2026-10-01, page read: numerical value 6.626 070 15 x 10^-34 J Hz^-1, standard uncertainty (exact), source 2022 CODATA recommended values.

codata-c.cite: NIST, CODATA Value: speed of light in vacuum (2022 CODATA recommended values).

codata-e.cite: NIST, CODATA Value: elementary charge (2022 CODATA recommended values).
codata-e.checked: 2026-10-01, page read: 1.602 176 634 x 10^-19 C, exact. Also read the Planck constant in eV/Hz page (4.135 667 696... x 10^-15 eV Hz^-1) as a cross-check of h / e.

os-up3-6-2.cite: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, section 6.2 Photoelectric Effect.
os-up3-6-2.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, as stated on the page; facts cited in our own words, no text copied
os-up3-6-2.checked: 2026-10-01, page text read: a photon is a particle of light, each photon moves at the speed of light and carries an energy quantum; the energy of a photon is E = hf (equation 6.13), where h is Planck's constant.

os-up2-16-5.cite: OpenStax University Physics Volume 2, section 16.5 The Electromagnetic Spectrum.
os-up2-16-5.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, as stated on the page; facts cited in our own words, no text copied
os-up2-16-5.checked: 2026-10-01, page text read: visible light is the narrow segment of the electromagnetic spectrum between about 400 nm and about 750 nm to which the normal human eye responds.

os-up3-1-5.cite: OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, section 1.5 Dispersion, Table 1.2.
os-up3-1-5.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, as stated on the page; facts cited in our own words, no text copied
os-up3-1-5.checked: 2026-10-01, page text read: for a given medium n increases as wavelength decreases and is greatest for violet light, so violet light is bent more than red light. Table 1.2 flint glass: 1.662 (660 nm), 1.665 (610), 1.667 (580), 1.674 (550), 1.684 (470), 1.698 (410).

os-bio-8-1.cite: OpenStax Biology 2e, section 8.1 Overview of Photosynthesis.
os-bio-8-1.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, as stated on the page; facts cited in our own words, no text copied
os-bio-8-1.checked: 2026-10-01, page text read: chloroplasts have a double membrane envelope (outer and inner membrane); within are stacked, disc-shaped thylakoids with chlorophyll embedded in the thylakoid membrane; a stack of thylakoids is a granum; the liquid-filled space around the granum is the stroma; the Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma.

os-bio-8-2.cite: OpenStax Biology 2e, section 8.2 The Light-Dependent Reactions of Photosynthesis.
os-bio-8-2.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, as stated on the page; facts cited in our own words, no text copied
os-bio-8-2.checked: 2026-10-01, page text read: shorter wavelengths are more powerful than longer wavelengths; chlorophyll a absorbs blue and red but not green, and because green is reflected or transmitted chlorophyll appears green; each photosystem is serviced by a light-harvesting complex of 300 to 400 chlorophyll a and b molecules plus carotenoids; absorbing a photon pushes a chlorophyll into an excited state; energy is transferred chlorophyll to chlorophyll until, after about a millionth of a second, it reaches the reaction center, and only energy, not electrons, moves up to that point; the PSII reaction center is P680; its missing electron is replaced from water; splitting one H2O releases two electrons, two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, and two are split for one O2; ATP and NADPH are made in the light-dependent reactions.

os-bio-4-2.cite: OpenStax Biology 2e, section 4.2 Prokaryotic Cells (Cell Size).
os-bio-4-2.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, as stated on the page; facts cited in our own words, no text copied
os-bio-4-2.checked: 2026-10-01, page text read: prokaryotic cells are 0.1 to 5.0 um in diameter, significantly smaller than eukaryotic cells, which have diameters ranging from 10 to 100 um.

os-bio-4-3.licence: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike, as stated on the page; facts cited in our own words, no text copied
os-bio-4-3.checked: 2026-10-01, page text read: plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and other specialized plastids, and a large central vacuole; chloroplasts are plant cell organelles that carry out photosynthesis.

astm-g173.cite: ASTM G173-03 Reference Solar Spectral Irradiance at Air Mass 1.5 (direct normal and hemispherical on a 37 degree tilted surface), distributed by NREL (Reference Air Mass 1.5 Spectra). Spectra modelled with SMARTS 2.9.2 (Gueymard).
astm-g173.licence: Reference data published by NREL for free use; the copied file is part of pvlib-python, BSD 3-Clause licence.
astm-g173.checked: 2026-10-01, nrel.gov did not answer from this machine, so the NREL page was read from the Internet Archive copy (web.archive.org/web/2024id_/...): G-173 is spectral irradiance in W m^-2 nm^-1 on an inclined plane at 37 degrees tilt facing the sun, absolute air mass 1.5, 1976 U.S. Standard Atmosphere, modelled with SMARTS2 2.9.2; columns are extraterrestrial, direct normal and global tilt. The CSV header reads 'ASTM G173-03 Reference Spectra Derived from SMARTS v. 2.9.2' with columns wavelength, extraterrestrial, global, direct. Used: global (as 'solar') and extraterrestrial (as 'space').

pcad.cite: PhotochemCAD 2.1a spectra (Du, H., Fuh, R. A., Li, J., Corkan, A. and Lindsey, J. S. (1998) Photochem. Photobiol. 68, 141-142; Dixon, J. M., Taniguchi, M. and Lindsey, J. S. (2005) Photochem. Photobiol. 81, 212-213), as published by S. Prahl at OMLC: Chlorophyll a in diethyl ether (123) and Chlorophyll b in diethyl ether (125).
pcad.licence: No licence is stated on the OMLC pages (site footer: Copyright 2018 Scott Prahl and Steve Jacques). Measured data are cited to the original PhotochemCAD papers and OMLC here and in the page credits; open question logged.
pcad.checked: 2026-10-01, both pages and both data files read: absorption measured by J. Li on 1997-12-11 with a Cary 3, 1.0 nm bandwidth; chlorophyll a scaled to a molar extinction of 111,700 cm^-1 M^-1 at 427.8 nm (Strain, Thomas and Katz 1963); chlorophyll b scaled to 159,100 cm^-1 M^-1 at 453.0 nm (Vernon and Seely 1966). Peaks found by tools/light_build.py: a 427.75 and 660.06 nm, b 453.0 and 643.0 nm.

cie1931.cite: CIE 2019, Colour-matching functions of CIE 1931 standard colorimetric observer, International Commission on Illumination (CIE), Vienna. DOI 10.25039/CIE.DS.xvudnb9b. File: CIE 1931 2-deg XYZ CMFs, 1 nm, from the Colour and Vision Research Laboratory (CVRL) database.
cie1931.licence: Standard reference data; cited by the DOI CIE asks for. No licence text was found on the CIE or CVRL pages.
cie1931.checked: 2026-10-01, CIE data table page read (how to cite, DOI) and the CVRL colour matching functions index read (CIE 1931 2-deg XYZ CMFs listed); CSV read: 360 to 830 nm at 1 nm, columns wavelength, x, y, z.

w3c-color4.cite: W3C CSS Color Module Level 4, sample code for colour conversions: XYZ_to_lin_sRGB matrix and the sRGB transfer function (gam_sRGB).

pdb-2bhw.cite: RCSB PDB 2BHW, Pea light-harvesting complex II at 2.5 angstrom resolution.
pdb-2bhw.checked: 2026-10-01, RCSB entry record read (data.rcsb.org/rest/v1/core/entry/2BHW): resolution 2.5 A, primary citation Standfuss et al. 2005. mmCIF read by tools/light_build.py: chains A, B, C (one trimer in the file, PQS assembly 'trimeric', identity operator), 24 CLA (chlorophyll a) and 18 CHL (chlorophyll b) with 42 magnesium atoms, carotenoids 6 LUX (lutein), 3 NEX (neoxanthin), 3 XAT (violaxanthin), 223 alpha carbons per chain.

standfuss-2005.cite: Standfuss, J., Terwisscha van Scheltinga, A. C., Lamborghini, M. and Kuhlbrandt, W. (2005). Mechanisms of photoprotection and nonphotochemical quenching in pea light-harvesting complex at 2.5 A resolution. EMBO J. 24, 919-928.
standfuss-2005.checked: 2026-10-01, abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 15719016): the 2.5 A structure of pea LHC-II shows the arrangement of 42 chlorophylls a and b, 12 carotenoids and six lipids in the LHC-II trimer; spectral assignment of individual chlorophylls indicates the flow of energy; the structure shows the complex in a quenched state.

liu-2004.cite: Liu, Z., Yan, H., Wang, K. et al. (2004). Crystal structure of spinach major light-harvesting complex at 2.72 A resolution. Nature 428, 287-292.
liu-2004.checked: 2026-10-01, abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 15029188): the 14 chlorophylls in each monomer are eight Chla and six Chlb; all Chlb are located around the interface between adjacent monomers; four carotenoid-binding sites per monomer.

mirkovic-2017.cite: Mirkovic, T., Ostroumov, E. E., Anna, J. M., van Grondelle, R., Govindjee and Scholes, G. D. (2017). Light Absorption and Energy Transfer in the Antenna Complexes of Photosynthetic Organisms. Chem. Rev. 117, 249-293.
mirkovic-2017.checked: 2026-10-01, abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 27428615): sunlight is captured by a network of light-absorbing pigments that funnel the excitation energy to the reaction centres; the review describes electronic excitation energy transfer (EET) and how coupling depends on the spatial and energetic landscape of the pigments.

croce-2014.cite: Croce, R. and van Amerongen, H. (2014). Natural strategies for photosynthetic light harvesting. Nat. Chem. Biol. 10, 492-501.
croce-2014.checked: 2026-10-01, abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 24937067): organisms adapt their pigmentation to the light in their habitat, acclimate to slow changes in light intensity and respond rapidly to fast changes; an overdose of light with oxygen can be lethal.

fret.licence: Wikipedia text licence applies to the article; only facts are used here, no text copied.
fret.checked: 2026-10-01, article source read: a donor chromophore in its excited state may transfer energy to an acceptor through nonradiative dipole-dipole coupling; the efficiency is inversely proportional to the sixth power of the distance between donor and acceptor; 'Forster resonance energy transfer' is preferred because the transfer is always nonradiative.

terashima-2009.cite: Terashima, I., Fujita, T., Inoue, T., Chow, W. S. and Oguchi, R. (2009). Green light drives leaf photosynthesis more efficiently than red light in strong white light: revisiting the enigmatic question of why leaves are green. Plant Cell Physiol. 50, 684-697.
terashima-2009.checked: 2026-10-01, abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 19246458): green light can penetrate further into the leaf than red or blue light; leaves use chlorophylls that absorb green light weakly, modify mesophyll structure and adjust the Rubisco to chlorophyll ratio.
